chapterNotes.1nephi|1:
This chapter really sets the stage for the Book of Mormon. We have Lehi, who is essentially an Old Testament prophet, at the same time as Jeremiah, during the rule of Zedekiah (verse 4), and he is stepping out of the narrative we find in the Old Testament, and into the narrative we have in the Book of Mormon. Many things in chapter 1 alone connect Lehi and his family to the time, like learning the language of the Egyptians which was prevalent around Jerusalem at the time (verse 2) or the prophesying of the destruction of Jerusalem (verse 18) which happened shortly thereafter. God is the same yesterday, today, and forever, and the experiences of Lehi solidify this. Even just his rejection as a prophet is something that is seen in the Old Testament, New Testament, and into the Restoration and recorded in Doctrine and Covenants.

Like many before and after them, Lehi and his son, Nephi, kept records which are now made available to us in the Book of Mormon, starting with this chapter. Why God chose for these specific records to be the ones made available to us is not known. It can be assumed that there were a number of other righteous people or religious leaders that have records from a similar time frame that could be of value to us. But what I do know, from this chapter alone, is that Lehi was a good man (verse 1), an inspired spiritual leader (verse 6-8) that received revelation, a person that was humble and led by the spirit (verse 12) and was full of gratitude (verse 15), and was a person of action (verse 19-20). On top of that, we have a diverse family unit, to which we can relate, and through which we can learn. Lehi and his family certainly seem like prime candidates to have records of in order for God to get his message through.
chapterNotes.1nephi|2:
The contrast between Nephi and Laman and Lemuel starts to take shape. Lehi makes it a point to talk to Laman and Lemuel about being steadfast and obedient (verse 9-10) to try to soften them and teach them, but they continued to murmur. We don’t know if Lehi also spoke to Nephi in a similar manner, but we know later on in the chapter (verse 16) that Nephi proactively wants to learn and feel the spirit. He takes it upon himself to pray and as a result he gets answers and is blessed (verse 19).

The pattern that starts to take shape is that obedience and gratitude to the Lord leads to blessings and prosperity, and that disobedience and complaint drive away the spirit and bring sadness (verse 20-23). Lehi is told to leave his home and immediately does so (obedience), and then upon leaving and making it to the wilderness he builds an alter (verse 7) and gives thanks (gratitude).

None of this is to be mistaken with living a life free from challenge. Lehi and his children are far from living a life without challenge, but the Lord strengthens them in the challenges and delivers them. Lehi and Nephi are exceptionally blessed throughout their lives due to their striving to be obedient, but they face their fair share of trials.
chapterNotes.1nephi|3:
Obedience and faith. Nephi is not hesitant to do what he is told and has the faith that if it’s something coming from the Lord that he will have the strength to do it (verse 7). He likely got to this point in his life by praying and striving to be close to Lord. We already know from chapter 2 that he is desirous to know the things of the Lord and that he supports his father as the prophet.

It’s interesting the failure that God lets Nephi and his brothers have. Additionally, it’s interesting that Nephi is able to convince Laman and Lemuel to persist despite their lack of faith. We know that Nephi is willing to persist because of his desire to be obedient and because of his faith in the Lord to eventually provide the way, so the question is, are the failures to test the level of Nephi’s faith, or are the failures more to test or teach Laman and Lemuel? If nothing else, their failures teach us. It may not make sense that Laman is the first of the brothers to attempt to get the plates (verse 11-14), after all neither Laman nor Lemuel even wanted to go in the first place. Nephi likely should have volunteered to make the attempt first. But what do we learn from the first failure? Do we learn that if we want to follow the Lord sometimes there is a right and a wrong way to do it, and perhaps casting lots was not the right way? Is the failure just setting the stage for teaching persistence? It could very well be both. This was something important that the Lord wanted accomplished, and they left it up to chance, casting lots on who would go. They seemingly didn’t have much of a plan, which we frequently need. We will not likely accidentally follow the will of God, it takes thought and effort. God wants us to CHOOSE to follow Him and make it a deliberate part of our lives, and they didn’t do that. They left it up to chance, and then sent one of the least dedicated members of the party.

The second failure leads to the losing of all their wealth (verse 24-26). Sometimes following the Lord will require sacrifice. Sacrifice of worldly goods, sacrifice of time, and even sacrifice of self. In this case, there are 2 angles to this. They were willing exchange all their worldly wealth to get these plates of brass. They esteemed (or Nephi and Lehi did) obedience to the Lord over worldly things and demonstrated it by gathering up their riches and then taking them to Laban. The other angle to this, is they were attempting to sacrifice something that they had already sacrificed. They left their riches behind already, and then attempted to use an already lost wealth as a demonstration of their sacrifice to the Lord. Perhaps God was showing them that giving up something already lost isn’t a large enough sacrifice for something this important. The willingness was there, but the value to the Lord perhaps wasn’t. What are we willing to give up or sacrifice to follow God? Are we gathering up our best “riches” or offering something of less value? Are we demonstrating to God the importance of His role in our lives?

Another important thing to remember is that Laman went to Laban first. And both Laman and Lemuel were there when they got the riches and tried to barter with Laban. They were present, but was that good enough? An angel visited them just a short time later (verse 29-31) and they still continued to doubt and murmur. They went through all the same actions as Nephi in this chapter, and arguably more because Laman went alone, but yet they had less faith and less desire. They were going through the actions. Laman probably half-heartedly asked Laban for the plates. Laman and Lemuel likely complained about gather up their riches. The Lord sees our hearts and knows our desires, and can tell when the actions we are doing don’t align. And sometimes they won’t always align, and we will be Lamans and Lemuels, just going through the motions. Which is better than a full abandonment of the Lord. But we should be striving to be like Nephi. Full of faith, obedient and desirous to follow the Lord even if it means sacrificing, and even it means failing and persisting.
chapterNotes.1nephi|4:
Obedience above all. The parallel of the story of Nephi and the story of Saul in the Old Testament is interesting. Saul was commanded to go smite everyone one in Amalek but spared the king and the best sheep and oxen saying that they were to sacrifice to Lord. But God did not ask Saul to save animals for sacrifice or spare the king. “… to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams.” Saul lost his appointment as king as a result of his lack of strict obedience to command of the Lord.

Nephi was similarly commanded to kill Laban. In fact, the spirit had to tell Nephi 3 times because he was so hesitant (verses 10-12). It may seem that God doesn’t give us that same patience that he gave to Nephi, but He most certainly does. Think of the number of times that the prophets and apostles have seemingly said the same things… why? Why do we re-read the scriptures over and over again? Why does the same topic in church get covered every 4 years and spoken about even more frequently over the pulpit? It takes time for us to take something to heart and truly learn it and become obedient to it.

But why was it so important for Nephi to kill Laban? I’m not sure why it was important to kill him versus just obtaining the plates in another way, but we do learn that the Lord will slay the wicked if they are standing in the way of righteous purposes (verses 13). But it was important for Nephi to get the plates… because of obedience. Nephi knew it was important to be obedient and that it led to prosperity, but how could they be obedient if they didn’t know what they needed to be obedient to? The law was on those plates. So in order to order to help his people be obedient forevermore, Nephi did obey the command to kill Laban (verses 14-18).

Zoram was also given the chance to display obedience. Once he realized that he wasn’t with Laban he got scared and was ready to leave until Nephi explained to him the circumstances. Nephi explained that they were commanded of God to do this thing and that they would have Zoram join them (verses 34-35). He could have run or fought, and my initial instinct is that he only went with them out of fear, but we learn through reading further in the BOM that Zoram stays faithful the whole time to Nephi, so whether he went out of fear or because he felt it was the obedient thing to do, he stayed obedient from that point forward.
chapterNotes.1nephi|5:
It’s interesting in this chapter to see the first instance of a person that we see as good and righteous having a moment of weakness and doubt. Sariah complains and extends her complaints to blaming Lehi for the potential loss of their sons, accusing him in a seeming negative way of being a visionary man. But this doesn’t make Sariah any less righteous or faithful person, what it makes her is a human. A fallible person that is prone to doubt. And when her sons return she even acknowledges that she is wrong and that God is good and that her husband is guided by the Lord (verse 8). It doesn’t say it explicitly, but it’s almost as if this is her repenting.

Another thing that stands out in this chapter is that they yet Again offer sacrifices in gratitude to God (verse 9). In all of the Book of Mormon there are only a couple references to people making sacrifices to God, and 3 of the are Lehi. This happens to be the second time we read about it. Despite losing all their riches and moving out of their home and fearing that their sons may die in effort to get the brass plates, they are still grateful and living in high spirits.

Lastly, this chapter confirms the great worth of the brass plates. Nephi killed Laban to get them, and the spirit emphasized how important it was that they get these records. We learn that the plates have a genealogy, and that they contain the prophecies of the prophets, and that they have the commandments. Lehi, being filled with the spirit, prophesies that they will go unto all nations (verse 18). Scriptures are of great worth to us if we let them be (verse 21) and they can provide us with the guidance we need. We have the Bible and the Book of Mormon and other scriptures, but we also have the words of modern day prophets, which is the same thing that went into scriptures of old. We should value these words with as much worth as the scriptures. With as much worth as Nephi and Lehi valued the brass plates.
chapterNotes.1nephi|6: In case we doubted the importance of the words found in the scriptures after Nephi risked his life and took the life of another man to get the brass plates, we now learn that Nephi set apart these plates, the ones that become the Book of Mormon, to be just for the things of the greatest worth and value unto us (verse 3, 5). It isn’t cluttered with unneeded things and confusing stories. So with that in mind, as we read through the verses of the Book of Mormon we can ask ourselves, “why was this written?”, “why is this considered of value?”, “what about this would be pleasing to God?”
chapterNotes.1nephi|7:
Patience, faith, and love. Nephi is a great example of these Christlike attributes. We don’t know the specifics of how Laman and Lemuel reacted to going back to Jerusalem to find wives, but they had previous been hesitant to go for the brass plates. However on their way back from Jerusalem Laman and Lemuel and now many of the children of Ishmael rebel against Nephi. They get it into their minds that they would have been better off in Jerusalem because they forgot. (Verses 10-12) 

We are asked to remember time and time again throughout the scriptures. In fact the word appears about 158 times throughout the Book of Mormon. In the sacrament prayers, both the bread and the water, we are agreeing to always remember him. This might be important, to remember the Lord, to remember His love and His power and His blessings. But why? What happens when we forget? We revert back to our old behaviors. All people need to go through a change, a conversion, put off the natural man. As Alma asks, “have ye experienced this mighty change in your hearts?” (Alma 5:14) and “can ye feel so now?” (Alma 5:26). There is a before and an after, and we will revert back to the natural man, to the before if we do not remember “what great things the Lord hath done for us” and “that the Lord is able to do all things”.

When Laman and Lemuel get mad at Nephi, they tie him up and how does Nephi respond? He prays. He doesn’t yell at his brothers (that we know of) or try to resort to his own strength to overcome the situation, he turns to the Lord. And because he turns to the Lord instead of retaliating, it drives the daughters of Ishmael to help soften the hearts of Laman and Lemuel which leads them to be sorrowful (verses 19-20). And what does Nephi then do? Forgives them. And not just forgives them, but “did frankly forgive them” (verse 21).Patience, did not get mad or retaliate. Faith, turned to the Lord for help and strength. Love, he forgave his brethren. This is the pattern to follow in times of trial or difficulty, Nephi laid it out for us. Be patient, exercise your faith, and increase your love.
chapterNotes.1nephi|8:
Lehi’s vision of the Tree of Life. There are so many directions to go with a study of this vision. We learn of the great joy and delightfulness in the love of God, and that Christ is the manifestation of God’s love. Partaking of the fruit of Christ or Christ’s Atonement will feel us with exceedingly great joy. We learn about the different patterns of life that people take, some failing to find their way, others finding it and then losing it, some finding themselves faithful, and then falling to the struggles of the world, others staying faithful and continually partaking of the joy of Christ, but lastly others that find themselves immediately going to the things of the world, and never truly trying. We learn about the word of God being the way to find true guidance and direction in our lives, and that listening and harkening to the word of God is the same grasping the iron rod. We learn about the way to following on the path to God is a strait and narrow way, meaning that God’s way is more direction-ed and intent-filled than the world’s.

Something that stood out to me this time though was the desire that Lehi felt after partaking of the fruit. He said the fruit was desirable and then he said that he desired that his family should eat the fruit too. Desire, to me, is at the root of it all. It leads to action. When something is desirable, like the fruit of the tree of life, people will be willing to work to obtain it. When someone desires something, it leads to action. Action is a part of faith, because we know faith without works is dead. Our acting is our demonstration that we have faith. Therefore we know that the love and Atonement of Christ is desirable, and that it is Christ in whom we should have faith. And we truly have faith in Christ, we will act in a way that demonstrates this faith, by adhering to His word, the word of God. Thus we will cling to the rod of iron. Our desire will lead to action, our action will strengthen and demonstrate our faith, and our faith will lead us to Christ.
chapterNotes.1nephi|9:
Nephi is commanded to make 2 sets of plates, one for the ministry or more spiritual things, and one for the reigns of the kings, or more historical temporal things.

What is significant in this chapter is what Nephi says to close the chapter (verses 5-6) that he doesn’t know why he’s received this commandment, but that he knows it must be for a wise purpose, because God knows all things and will do what is needed to accomplish his work. We need to apply this principle in our lives more. We don’t understand what God understands but yet stubbornly work to accomplish our own will so often rather than just relying on the guidance of the Lord and trusting that His direction is the right direction.
chapterNotes.1nephi|10: The meat of this chapter feels like verses 17-19. We know that Lehi prophesied a lot to his family and others, because he was a prophet and closet to the spirit. And not that the words and content of his revelations are not important in this chapter, but what stands out is Nephi’s response to it all. Nephi was desirous To know by the power of the Holy Ghost the same things his father did (verse 17). And then Nephi makes it clear to everyone that the ability to obtain this knowledge through the Holy Ghost is not an exclusive ability. Nephi is a man of great of faith and strength and his father is the prophet, but it doesn’t take being a prophet or being Nephi. All who diligently seek shall find (verse 19) and the Lord is unchanging (verse 18). So when we read these things in the Book of Mormon or Bible and think that it was just because these people lived in a different time that they were able to get such clear direction from the Lord, we can’t forget that the it’s same God then as now, and he is constant and consistent. We just need to do our part and exercise the needed faith and effort.
chapterNotes.1nephi|11:
This is where the vision that Lehi had starts to come into clearer view. It’s all centered around the love of God and His desire to bless us. In verse 10 the spirit asks Nephi what he desires. God grants according to desires, He looks upon the heart. And that may make us wonder why then does not everyone get blessed with everything they want… God grants according to righteous desire and faith. Some people truly do desire things that God would prefer not to offer. In this case, Nephi desires to understand the vision.

The first part of clarity we come across is the meaning of the tree. The spirit asks Nephi about what he knows of God, and his answer is one that has stuck with me for many years: “I know that he loveth his children; nevertheless, I do not know the meaning of all things.” (Verse 17) If there is one thing to understand before worrying about understanding all the others, it is that God loves all of us. We are His literal children and He loves us all perfectly. That truth alone is worth more than any worldly knowledge that one can gain. The love of god is the tree.

Something to remember is that Nephi is seeing this vision of Christ and His life and earthly ministry, and this is all before Christ. He is seeing something is yet to happen, he just has faith Christ will come. This vision solidifies to him the level of the love that Christ has for His people. Not that he didn’t know Christ was full of love before and based revelations that he had access to in the brass plates, it would have at least been assumed that Christ was full of love, but now he knows it in a different and more complete way. And so should we.
chapterNotes.1nephi|12:
Nephi sees the destruction of his people in this chapter. They go from 3 consecutive generations of complete righteousness to being completely overtaken within the span of a couple hundred years. This seems baffling until you think of the evolution of our world from generation to generation. Even just 50 years, some of the things in the world today would be unthinkable. But the crazy thing is that through all of time and generations God is unmoved. He is always there with the same path leading back to Him, it is us that moves, that distances ourselves from Him. Verse 19 talks about how because Nephi’s people were full of pride and fell to the temptations of the devil, which is what allowed them to be overtaken. It takes continual diligence and work to stay on the righteous path. It’s like walking the opposite direction of a moving sidewalk. The only way to avoid being further from your destination (in this case God) is to continually move, because even just pausing or lazily sauntering won’t be good enough.

The other thing learned in this chapter is the appearance of Christ to the people of Nephi. We know that the people of Nephi will occupy the land of the Americas, so even before making it to 3 Nephi, we know that Christ will appear. Which makes sense… there are more than just people in the old world of Jerusalem, and God loves ALL of His children, so why couldn’t Christ visit as many people as He could?
chapterNotes.1nephi|13:
The Lord set apart the land of America (verse 12). It was foretold many generations before the true founding of America and establishment of America. The religious freedom that America gave people was critical for the restoration of the gospel and all started with people fleeing religious persecution in other parts of the world (verse 16). With more religious freedom came the broader use of the Bible among non-clergy allowing people to learn the gospel for themselves (verses 23-28) causing religious stirring in the US and around the world. Think, in the time of Joesph Smith how many different religions there were in such a small and non-populous area. Everyone was reading the bible and making their interpretations of it. In part, this was driven by the perverting of the bible that those who had held power over translation and publication may have had (verses 29). Everyone was trying to do their best and follow God, but only could go so far without the full and clear truth of the gospel. This is what leads to the restoration and the coming forth of the Book of Mormon (verses 34-36). This chapter is a true treasure of world and religious history. Religious persecution -> fleeing -> arrival in a “new world” ordained by God -> religious excitement -> Joseph Smith -> restoration of the gospel. The Lord knows the beginning from the end. We may not know the extent to which Nephi saw all this, but the Lord knew what was coming. Lastly is the bringing forth of the Book of Mormon and other scriptures (verses 39-40).

We need never doubt the Lord nor His Plan. He knows the beginning from the end and His work will not be hindered. Look at all the events in history that need to occur for the right conditions to exist for the restoration of the gospel. Nothing is coincidence.
